 Larry Magid: From insurance to elections, how scammers exploit current events
 Larry Magid
 PUBLISHED: October 22, 2026 at 8:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 22, 2026 at 10:18 AM PDT 
 Categories: 
 Business , Latest Headlines , News 
 Online scams have been with us for years, and many of the oldies but baddies are still around. But scammers pay attention to current events and constantly find new ways to separate people from their money and private information.
 Whether it’s fake donation sites after natural disasters, bogus investment opportunities tied to new technology, phony government benefit programs or “too good to be true” holiday shopping deals, scammers are quick to capitalize on the news.
 Two current events especially attractive to scammers right now are health insurance open enrollment and the upcoming elections. But they’re hardly the only opportunities scammers are exploiting.
 Health insurance scams We’re now in the Medicare open enrollment period, which runs through December 7, and the Affordable Care Act open enrollment period is approaching. These events make it open season for scammers and dishonest businesses looking to take advantage of people searching for better deals, especially as insurance premiums rise and some government subsidies are reduced.
 The Federal Trade Commission has issued a consumer alert warning that scammers sometimes pay to have their websites appear near the top of search results. The FTC warns that “Bad actors often use web addresses that look similar to government website addresses.” They also use official-looking logos and search keywords to impersonate HealthCare.gov or Medicare.gov.
 Clicking one of these ads or calling its phone number could lead you to a bogus plan that isn’t legitimate health insurance or expose you to medical identity theft .
 Another common scam, said Doug Shadel, a former fraud investigator with the Washington State Attorney General’s Office, involves callers pretending to represent Medicare. They ask, “Did you get the new Medicare card we sent out?” If the answer is no, they claim you must provide identifying information or risk losing your Medicare benefits.
 If you need information or assistance, the FTC advises people to go directly to Medicare.gov or call 1-800-633-4227 for Medicare coverage, and to HealthCare.gov or call 1-800-318-2596 for Affordable Care Act plans. Rather than clicking a link, type the web address yourself and double-check that you’ve entered it correctly.
 If you’re shopping for private insurance, Medicare Advantage or a Medicare supplement, make sure you’re dealing with a legitimate insurer or reputable broker. Double-check the web address to avoid impersonators or businesses other than the one you’re seeking.
 Election scams and misinformation With Election Day approaching, scammers are using old and new tricks to spread misinformation, solicit fraudulent donations and steal personal information. Criminals can impersonate candidates and campaigns, using AI-generated voices, images and fake fundraising appeals. Between now and Nov. 3, be especially careful to make sure any donation goes to the candidate or cause you want to support, rather than a scammer or impersonator. Visit the campaign’s official website rather than clicking links in unsolicited emails, texts or social media posts.
 But not all election-related deception is about stealing money. Some is designed to influence what people believe about candidates and issues.
 Manipulated political images are nothing new. During the 2004 presidential election, a photograph circulated online that appeared to show Democratic candidate John Kerry sharing a podium with actress and antiwar activist Jane Fonda at a Vietnam War protest. It was a fake, combining two separate photographs. That was long before generative AI made convincing fake images and videos accessible to almost anyone.
 During this year’s campaign, an AI-generated video falsely depicted a Texas candidate calling for higher taxes, including a tax on brisket, enough to anger almost any meat-loving Texan, regardless of political affiliation. Another fake AI-generated image supposedly showed someone stuffing a California ballot box. These are only two of many examples of AI-generated campaign ads meant to deceive rather than inform.
 Some AI-generated images have been traced to official political campaigns, but many are posted by others, including individuals and groups with their own agendas, scammers and even foreign governments.
 Even after the election, don’t believe everything you see or hear about the results. Check reputable news organizations and official results from state and local election officials before accepting claims about who won or allegations of election fraud. Be especially skeptical of calls to protest results or donate to post-election legal battles based on claims unsupported by credible evidence.
 Farm equipment scams offer lessons for all shoppers Even if you’re not a farmer, it’s worth paying attention to recent scams targeting this hardworking group, many of whom are struggling with rising diesel prices and the financial impact of tariffs. The lessons apply to just about any online purchase.
 The FTC reports that scammers are posing as legitimate agricultural equipment dealers, advertising tractors and other expensive equipment through social media and search engines, often using real business names. They send professional-looking invoices and purchase agreements and demand deposits or full payment, often by wire transfer. But the equipment never arrives, and the seller disappears or makes excuses.
 Before buying from an unfamiliar website, search the company’s name along with words like “scam” or “complaint,” and independently verify its website and phone number. Don’t assume a sponsored ad is legitimate because it uses a real business’s name.
 Whatever you’re shopping for, be suspicious of sellers who insist on wire transfers, gift cards or cryptocurrency, since those payments can be difficult or impossible to recover. Credit cards generally offer stronger fraud protections, including the ability to dispute charges. Debit cards also offer protections, but your liability can depend on how quickly you report a problem, and missing funds may take time to recover. Apple Pay and Google Pay purchases generally retain the protections of the linked credit or debit card.
 And don’t forget the scams that have been around for years, including fake lottery winnings, bogus tech support calls, romance scams and variations of those infamous Nigerian prince emails promising a fortune.
 Scammers may change their stories to keep up with the headlines, but the warning signs are often the same. A little skepticism and a few minutes spent checking things out can save you a lot of money and trouble.
